_design: All verified + refuted across CLOSED researches.

verified_findings.claim: OCEL 2.0 is the foundational standard for object-centric process mining: it extends OCEL 1.0 with Object-to-Object (O2O) relations alongside Event-to-Object (E2O) relations, qualifiers on both relation types, and time-varying (dynamic) object attributes, letting a single event reference multiple objects of different types and removing the single-case-concept constraint.

OCEL 2.0 ships a comprehensive specification (metamodel + formalization) plus three concrete exchange formats — SQLite (relational), XML, and JSON — along with example datasets, libraries, and software tools.

OCEL 2.0 enables on-demand, multi-perspective process mining from a single unchanging data source — eliminating repeated data extraction when the analytical question/perspective changes — and structurally avoids the convergence (event duplication across cases) and divergence (inability to separate causally-unrelated events) distortions inherent to single-case-object approaches.

A formal object-centric conformance-checking method exists — 'object-centric Petri nets with identifiers' (OPID) — combining object-centric Petri nets (one-to-many relations) with Petri nets with identifiers (object identity comparison), enabling conformance alignments that track object identity and inter-object dependencies. Implemented as the oCoCoMoT tool with alignments encoded as SMT.

ATC + Code Inspector (SCI) is the SAP-native static-analysis engine for custom code; SCI is the underlying check engine and ATC the management/front-end layer that integrates Code Inspector checks into a single tool. The S/4HANA readiness analysis runs the SCI check variant named S4HANA_READINESS_<Version>, selected as the Check Variant when configuring ATC runs, and scopes by namespace (Z*/Y* package ranges plus any additional custom-code package, with customer /XYZ/ namespaces requiring registration via SE03 + SATC_AC_INIT_NAMESPACE_REG).
verified_findings.vote: merged claims [9],[10],[23],[24] — unanimous 3-0 except [24] which was 2-1 but independently corroborated by SAPinsider + SAP Help
sources: help.sap.com Registering Name Spaces at the ATC Master System

verified_findings.claim: ATC supports a centralized remote code-analysis architecture: one central ATC check system (SAP_BASIS >=7.51/7.52, holding the latest checks and the Simplification Database) can remotely check custom ABAP code in many managed/satellite systems running on various NetWeaver AS ABAP releases (SAP_BASIS 7.00 SP15+, 7.01, 7.02, 7.31, 7.40, 7.50+) via RFC stubs. This means a code-mining brain can scan the whole landscape from a single hub rather than per-system. ATC can also be wired into the transport release process so only NEW/changed objects in a transport are checked and the request can be BLOCKED on findings (configured via SE03/SPRO), linking code-quality to the change lifecycle.
verified_findings.vote: merged claims [11],[12] — unanimous 3-0; central-checker 7.51/7.52 vs checked-system 7.00+ distinction noted
sources: help.sap.com Remote Code Analysis in ATC with a Central Check System (SAP_NETWEAVER_AS_ABAP_752)
help.sap.com Setting Up ATC Transport Checking

verified_findings.claim: S/4HANA custom-code readiness analysis is driven by the Simplification Database — a table in the S/4HANA system containing all Simplification Items, each describing a changed/removed SAP object and referring to a dedicated SAP Note that explains impact and how to adapt the custom code. The Simplification Database must be loaded into the central ATC check system; the ATC S4HANA_READINESS checks run against it. Displayed/checked via transaction SYCM (Simplification Item Check); imported per SAP KBA 3693326.

Runtime usage measurement of custom objects is mined from SAP's statistical sources: ABAP Call Monitor (transaction SCMON) collects execution data of programs/function modules/method calls; transaction SUSG aggregates/persists it (SCMON retains only ~7 days locally); UPL (Usage Procedure Logging) is the predecessor whose data is stored in SAP Solution Manager BW; and ST03/ST03N (SWNC workload statistics) supplies TRANSACTION usage / last-used dates that UPL/SCMON cannot capture. SAP recommends collecting at least one year (ideally up to ~13 months, to span quarter/year-end cycles) of production usage data. SCMON/SUSG is SAP's documented successor to UPL.
verified_findings.vote: merged claims [1],[7],[16],[22] — unanimous 3-0; '13 months' is a best-practice ceiling not a hard requirement
sources: community.sap.com SUSG aggregate usage data blogs

verified_findings.claim: It is an established industry heuristic that 40%-60% of custom code objects in a typical SAP system are no longer used (dead/unused), detectable via runtime usage data — making used-vs-unused and hot-vs-dead classification a high-value mining target. Some sources cite even higher (60-75% never called).
verified_findings.vote: unanimous 3-0 [21],[22], but secondary/vendor sourcing → medium confidence

verified_findings.claim: SAP's Custom Code Migration Fiori app is the central tool for usage-based scoping and supports three project types: (1) SAP S/4HANA Migration Project, (2) SAP BTP Analysis Project (cloud readiness), and (3) Custom Code Analysis Project for arbitrary ATC check variants (including dependency and complexity analyses). Usage-based scoping — fed by SCMON/SUSG or UPL production data — determines frequently-used code to migrate vs. unused code deleted via deletion transport requests during the SUM-driven system conversion. The end-to-end process is: custom code scoping + custom code analysis (preparatory) then custom code adaptation. Scoping is ONLY available in the Migration app, NOT the classic SAP GUI/remote-ATC path.

SAP Solution Manager 7.2 Custom Code Lifecycle Management (CCLM) is the central application managing custom code across the entire landscape from creation through decommissioning. Its usage evaluation requires BOTH workload statistics (ST03N) AND (UPL or SCMON) data in the managed system. CCLM includes a Decommissioning Cockpit covering a four-phase decommissioning process that identifies removal candidates by: non-usage over a defined period, similarity/clone-duplication to existing SAP objects, never being active in production, created long ago, and obsolescence due to standard functionality. (Note: SAP Cloud ALM is the strategic successor for custom code management, but CCLM remains the documented SolMan 7.2 capability.)
sources: help.sap.com Custom Code Retirement - Decommissioning Cockpit

verified_findings.claim: abaplint is an open-source (MIT-licensed) standalone static-analysis tool / linter for ABAP, written in TypeScript, that operates on code serialized via abapGit — making it a repository/code-side analysis tool usable in CI pipelines. It performs dead-code and unused-object detection via concrete rules: unused_variables (variables and constants), unused_methods (private/protected, excluding constructors/test/event handlers), unused_types, unused_macros, and unreachable_code (183 rules total) — directly relevant to dead-code detection and decommissioning use cases, and a graph-friendly open-source complement to SAP-native tooling.

Celonis connects to SAP ECC/S4HANA via a deployed, installable RFC ABAP module (a transport imported into SAP, requiring dev rights, with documented install/update/operations steps) acting as the bridge to the SAP DB — not direct DB access or pure external table reads. It also ships a separate SAP extraction client supporting legacy SAP 4.6C and PI/PO.

Celonis's primary SAP extraction mode is 'Continuous Extraction' — change-log-based (CDC-style) delta sync from ECC and S/4HANA (on-prem + private cloud) — distinct from one-time and local (in-system ABAP GUI report) extraction modes. Delta is implemented via RFC functions /CELONIS/EX_CL_NEW (filters to changed rows) and /CELONIS/EX_CL_SET_EXTRACTED (flags extracted records); a newer real-time Replication Cockpit also exists.

Celonis's Process Intelligence Graph (Process Sphere) is built on an object-centric data model (OCDM): foundational concepts are Objects, Events, and Relationships. A single object-centric dataset yields MULTIPLE process event logs via 'Perspectives' (each event log anchored to a single chosen object), rather than one fixed case notion — a genuine departure from classic single-case-table process mining.

Celonis documents handling of SAP cluster tables (specifically BSEG) as a dedicated best-practice topic titled 'Replacing SAP cluster tables (BSEG)' for object-centric process mining — addressing BSEG's compressed cluster storage (non-key columns in VARDATA inside RFBLG cluster).

UiPath Process Mining (ex-ProcessGold) native SAP extraction uses RFC: it requires S_RFC authorization for RFC destinations and calls standard function modules RFCPING, RFC_GET_FUNCTION_INTERFACE, RFC_READ_TABLE (plus FUNCTION_EXISTS) — but ALSO requires installing a CUSTOM ABAP function module Z_XTRACT_IS_TABLE (created via SE37, activated via SE80, needing an SAP user with a development key) on the SAP system itself. So it is an on-stack custom-extractor approach, not pure standard-RFC.

SAP Signavio Process Intelligence's native ABAP/SAP-ERP extraction method is the STANDARD RFC function module RFC_READ_TABLE (via the on-prem extractor using SAP JCo), supported on SAP Basis 7.40+ — i.e. the same generic primitive practitioners use, not a proprietary CDC stream. (Known 512-char/row limit fixed via SAP Note 2246160.) A newer SAP Datasphere Replication Flow path via CDS Views also exists as an alternative.

SAP Signavio Process Intelligence offers two integration models: 'Standardized data integration' (process performance data for SAP-defined business content from supported source systems pushed to the SAP BTP tenant at predefined intervals — the Process Insights / SAP-delivered-content path) vs 'Custom data integration' (cloud data pipelines extracting raw data and transforming it into an event log at custom intervals). In the custom path the table-to-event-log transformation is SQL-script-driven INSIDE Signavio (case-based and object-based pipelines; transformation scripts / 'event collectors' written in the SQL editor) — not delivered as raw extracts.

SAP Signavio Process Insights connects on-premise S/4HANA (and ECC/Business Suite) to the cloud tenant via the ST-PI plug-in (requiring ST-A/PI plug-ins) installed IN the SAP system — an on-stack ABAP plug-in, NOT an external cloud extractor. Data is PUSHED/triggered from within the SAP system over an encrypted outbound HTTPS connection to SAP BTP (leveraging the SAP Cloud ALM framework mechanism); setup via /n/SDF/PINS_SETUP or SDCCN. The SAP Cloud Connector is explicitly NOT needed and CANNOT be used.

SAP delivers STANDARD on-stack process-mining reference content: 'Sample Content for Process Mining on SAP S/4HANA – Purchase to Pay' runs on top of SAP Profitability and Performance Management (PaPM), a natively-integrated S/4HANA HANA add-on — NOT a separate cloud extractor. The extraction/connector method is replication of ERP tables into PaPM 'Model Table' functions (with an option to fetch from a remote SAP system), processed in-engine to derive activities, generate variant IDs, rank variants, and add START/END activities. Reads ACDOCA/COSP/COSS directly via HANA views (zero data movement). This is the SAP-delivered normative baseline / reference model.

The SAP P2P process-mining transformation layer (PaPM sample content) is built from a specific, named set of standard SAP ERP source tables: BKPF + BSEG (accounting docs), CDHDR + CDPOS (change documents), EKKO + EKPO (purchasing docs), EBAN (purchase requisitions), LFA1 (vendor master), T001 (company codes), USR02 (logon data). This is the checkable, SAP-official tables-to-event-log input mapping for P2P.

The academic object-centric approach (Berti, Park, Rafiei, van der Aalst — PADS, RWTH Aachen + Fraunhofer FIT, arXiv:2110.03467) extracts SAP event data into Object-Centric Event Logs (OCEL) as intermediate storage to AVOID pre-committing to a single case notion — explicitly contrasting commercial extractors (Celonis, ProcessGold) that require a fixed case notion and suffer convergence/divergence problems. It names concrete per-process target tables: EKKO/RBKP/EKBE for P2P and VBAK/BKPF for O2C, classifying EKPO/EKPA/EKET/EKBE/BSEG/RSEG/RESB as detail tables — a checkable academic SAP-table-to-event-log mapping.

PM4Py is the leading open-source Python process-mining library, managed/developed by PIS (Process Intelligence Solutions), a spinoff of the Fraunhofer Institute FIT where it was originally created. It is the open-source vehicle for the same OCEL/object-centric paradigm.

BP/CVI is mandatory for S/4HANA conversion: the Business Partner is the leading object and single entry point, completely replacing the ECC customer/vendor transactions; all customers, vendors and contacts must be synchronized to a BP. Authoritative sources are the CVI Cookbook (KBA 2713963) and SAP Note 2265093 (S4TWL - Business Partner Approach, which contains the BP conversion guide as attachment).

Standard CVI synchronization (Customer/Vendor → BP) creates BP roles FLVN00 and FLVN01 for suppliers/vendors and FLCU00 and FLCU01 for customers (FLxx00 = general/FI company data, FLxx01 = purchasing-org / sales-area data). The *01 roles are created only when purchasing-org / sales-area data exists in the source record.

Customer/vendor-to-BP links are stored in tables CVI_CUST_LINK (PARTNER_GUID↔KUNNR) and CVI_VEND_LINK (PARTNER_GUID↔LIFNR); the common key to BUT000 is PARTNER_GUID. Assigning the same number to BP and customer/vendor is recommended but optional (KBA 2430380).

Mass CVI synchronization is executed via transaction MDS_LOAD_COCKPIT. BP data-quality checks (postal code, geo code, mandatory field, tax number, bank data, tax jurisdiction, e-mail) in the Customer/Vendor→BP direction can be suppressed per SAP Note 2780288 (default BAdI CVI_CUSTOM_MAPPER); postal-code and address-regional checks are suppressed by default in normal (non-migration) synchronization.

Pre-conversion BP-readiness is assessed by the standard master-data consistency check report CVI_MIGRATION_PRECHK, run via transaction CVI_PRECHK or from the CVI Cockpit Preparation tab. It is meant to run early (Preparation phase) before CVI synchronization, listing all customer/vendor inconsistencies vs. the BP data model. Delivered as of ECC EhP8 SP12 and made available down to ECC 6.0 via SAP Note 2743494.

A CVI_MIGRATION_PRECHK result of 'All applied Checks (0/0)' means NO check was actually performed (e.g. selection yielded zero records), NOT that the data passed — a 0/0 outcome must never be scored as clean readiness. A genuine clean result requires checks to have run against selected data and returned zero errors.

The CVI_PRECHK error 'Tax Type XXX is not maintained for country YY' is caused by missing Tax Number Categories; the BP-conversion mapping requires a Tax Number Category defined for each customer/vendor country in the master data. Fixed in maintenance view V_TFKTAXNUMTYPE via SM30 (tables TFKTAXNUMTYPE / _C / _T; BP tax numbers stored in DFKKBPTAXNUM). Detect ahead of conversion via the CVI Master Data Consistency Check report in the CVI Cockpit or transaction CVI_PRECHK directly.

The CVI pre-check can be scoped by Customer/Vendor object (one at a time), Customer Number Range and Account Group, and by selecting specific or all business checks (Tax Code, Postal Code, Email, Transportation Zones, Tax Jurisdiction, Number Range, Industry, Bank Data, Address). This scoping is exactly what enables scoring BP-migration readiness from existing master data before conversion.

Maintenance Planner is the MANDATORY first technical step of the conversion: it checks add-ons, active business functions and industry solutions for S/4HANA compatibility and generates the stack.xml file that the Software Update Manager (SUM) requires as input. It replaced the Maintenance Optimizer, which S/4HANA does not support.

The Simplification Item Check (SI-Check) is run via standalone report /SDF/RC_START_CHECK in SA38 (select target S/4HANA version → 'Check Consistency for All' against the Simplification Item List). It is MANDATORY, runs without SAP Solution Manager, is re-triggered automatically by SUM (phases RUN_S4H_SIF_CHECK_INIT / _EXEC), and is a HARD GATE: all errors must be resolved/exempted before SUM can enter downtime (SUM stops on RC=12 at start, RC=8 or higher before downtime). Delivered by SAP Notes 2399707 (check report) and 2502552 (check classes via TCI); framework installed by following Note 2502552 in SNOTE.

SAP Readiness Check for S/4HANA identifies the simplification items relevant to a SPECIFIC ECC source system, derived from transactions used, customizing and table contents (run against production for accurate relevance). SAP Note 2913617 ('SAP Readiness Check for SAP S/4HANA') governs the conversion/migration scenario; SAP Note 3059197 ('SAP Readiness Check for SAP S/4HANA upgrades') governs the S/4HANA→S/4HANA upgrade scenario.

The conversion follows a fixed Prepare→Realize sequence. Prepare: Planning & System Requirements → Maintenance Planner → SI-Check → Custom Code Migration, with SAP Readiness Check 2.0 and the Simplification Item Catalog spanning it. Realize: SUM performs DB migration (to HANA, via DMO if not yet on HANA) + software update (ECC→S/4HANA) + the major part of data conversion in one tool, followed by cross-application and application-specific follow-on activities. SUM is the central conversion tool.

FINANCE specifics: in S/4HANA new Asset Accounting asset transactions are no longer stored in a technically separate FI-AA subledger (legacy tables ANEP/ANEA/ANEK/ANLC/ANLP no longer updated) but recorded directly in the Universal Journal ACDOCA, the same structure as G/L postings; FI and AA are unified in ACDOCA and the old GL↔AA reconciliation programs (RAABST01/02, FAA_GL_RECON) were removed. Legacy tables remain as compatibility views (FAAV_*).
sources: SAP Note 2270387 (S4TWL Data Structure Changes in Asset Accounting)

verified_findings.claim: The native SAP role/authorization data model is fully captured in AGR_* tables, enabling reconstruction of role-to-user and role-to-authorization-value links: AGR_DEFINE (role definitions, PARENT_AGR for derived roles), AGR_USERS (user-to-role assignment with FROM_DAT/TO_DAT validity), AGR_TCODES (role-to-transaction), AGR_1251 (role-level auth objects/authorizations/field values LOW/HIGH plus status MODIFIED), AGR_AGRS (composite-to-single role hierarchy), AGR_1016 (generated profile names). AGR_USERS joined to AGR_1251 is the canonical path to expand a role's effective authorization values.

Core user master, logon, and runtime authorization-value data live in USR*/UST12 tables: USR01 (user master/defaults), USR02 (logon data — password, lock, validity), USR04 (user master authorizations/profile assignment), USR12 (user master authorization VALUES), UST12 (user master: authorizations — the SUIM-reporting copy of USR12).

The SU24 transaction-to-authorization-object proposal/check model is stored in customer-specific tables USOBT_C and USOBX_C: USOBX_C holds the CHECK INDICATOR per transaction/object via field OKFLAG (N=Do not check, X=Always check, Y=Check + USOBT entry/proposal maintained); USOBT_C holds the proposed default authorization FIELD VALUES (FIELD/VON/BIS) for objects flagged as maintained. SU22 reads the SAP-delivered USOBT/USOBX; SU24 reads the customer _C copies — so an automated analyzer should mine USOBT_C/USOBX_C for the customer-effective role-generation proposals.

TSTCA is the table representing authorization objects checked at transaction START — values SAP evaluates automatically (kernel-level, before S_TCODE) when a transaction begins, distinct from in-program AUTHORITY-CHECK proposals in SU24. Fields OBJCT (auth object), FIELD, VALUE keyed by TCODE. It supplies the per-transaction object values needed to reconstruct who-can-execute-which-tcode-with-which-values.

A SU24/USOBX_C proposal does NOT enforce security — an authorization object is only actually checked at runtime if the program code contains a corresponding AUTHORITY-CHECK statement. USOBX_C can SUPPRESS a check (N/Do-not-check overrides code) but cannot CREATE enforcement where no AUTHORITY-CHECK exists. Therefore linking authorization objects to the programs/transactions that truly check them requires code inspection (AUTHORITY-CHECK, SU22/SU24) and/or runtime tracing — not USOBX_C alone.

Authorization checks and their field values are recorded at runtime via a system trace (ST01) or a dedicated authorization trace (STAUTHTRACE), which captures the authorization object, the checked authorization values, and the result, and supports per-user filtering (activate/evaluate/deactivate). This trace data is the input for maintaining SU22/SU24 default values (USOBT_C/USOBX_C proposals) AND for maintaining role menu/authorization data in PFCG — linking runtime AUTHORITY-CHECK calls back to role/SU24 maintenance.
sources: SAP Help Portal — Trace for Authorization Checks (help.sap.com/doc/saphelp_nw74)

verified_findings.claim: A SoD ruleset models risks at TWO levels — action (transaction) and permission (authorization object/field value). A Function is the building block: a task executed in SAP (e.g. purchase-order maintenance = ME21N+ME22N; vendor master maintenance) that groups transactions plus the authorization objects/values required to execute each. An SoD Risk = two or more conflicting Functions combined with an OR operator; risk fires when at least one qualifying action with its permission is found in each function. There are three risk types: Critical Action (single function of critical transactions), Critical Permission (single function of critical auth objects/permissions), and SoD Risk (conflicting functions).

In SAP GRC Access Control (Access Risk Analysis), the ruleset is a three-tier function→action→permission model stored in DDIC: GRACFUNC (Function master) + GRACFUNCT (descriptions), GRACFUNCACT (Function-Action/transaction Relationship), and GRACFUNCPRM (Function-Action-Permission Relationship — the auth-object/field-value tier carried as RESOURCEID + FROMVAL/TOVAL value range, with an ACTIVE=X flag). This is exactly the structure used to expand a user's effective authorizations against the ruleset.

In GRC Access Control, an SoD Risk header is stored in GRACSODRISK (field RISKTYPE: 1=SoD, 2=Critical Action, 3=Critical Permission; plus RISKLEVEL/ACTIVE), linked to its conflicting functions via GRACSODRISKFUNC (Risk-Function, keys RISKID/FUNCTID), assigned to a ruleset via GRACSODRISKRS, to systems via GRACSODRISKCONN, with descriptions in GRACSODRISKT and owners in GRACSODRISKOWN. The ruleset container is GRACRULESET + GRACRULESETT (descriptions). This normalized many-to-many model is why the junction tables exist (GRACSODRISK itself has no RULESETID/FUNCTID column).

The GRC ruleset is COMPILED (not hand-maintained) into executable rules: generated action/transaction-level rules in GRACACTRULE (SOD Action Rule Detail; keys RISKID/ACTRULEID/FUNCTID/CONNECTOR/ACTION) and organization-level rules in GRACORGRULE. The compilation is run by program/job GRAC_GENERATE_RULES whenever a ruleset changes. Risk-analysis results (violations) land in GRACUSERPRMVL (User Permission Violation Table; keys include USERID/RISKID/ACTRULEID/CONNECTOR), enabling direct extraction of who violates which risk.

MATERIAL LEDGER is mandatory in all S/4HANA systems (S4TWL note 2267834, component MM-IM-GF-VAL), independent of whether the source used Simple Finance or already ran ML. It is auto-activated during conversion (transactional inventory fields LBKUM/SALK3/VKSAL come from ACDOCA rather than legacy inventory tables), and ML data is migrated post-SUM in migration step M10. The technical data-model change (note 2354768) replaces legacy periodic tables MLHD/MLIT/MLPP/MLPPF/MLCR/MLCRF/MLKEPH/CKMLPP/CKMLCR/MLCD/CKMLMV003/CKMLMV004/CKMLPPWIP/CKMLKEPH with new tables MLDOC and MLDOCCCS (plus extract tables MLDOC_EXTRACT/MLDOCCCS_EXTRACT) and replaces CKMLMV011 with MLRUNLIST; SAP provides NO table-level compatibility views, so custom code referencing legacy ML tables must be reworked. Actual costing remains OPTIONAL — the migration does not activate it (toggled separately via CKMSTART/CKMLCP). READINESS ASSESSMENT: detect ML activation per valuation area (T001W/T001K, MGVUPD='X' for actual costing) and scan custom code for references to the obsolete ML* tables.
verified_findings.vote: merged from claims [0],[13],[14],[15],[16],[19],[20] — all unanimous 3-0 except [13] and [15] at 2-1

verified_findings.claim: The General Ledger move to the Universal Journal is governed by S4TWL note 2270339 (component FI-GL); incompatible changes to summary/index tables and to BSEG are documented in note 2431747 ('General Ledger: Incompatible Changes in S/4HANA compared to classic ERP releases'). At conversion New G/L is AUTOMATICALLY active (classic GL data is transferred into the new ACDOCA-based structures), but Document Splitting and Parallel Ledger functionality require a SEPARATE subsequent activation — they are NOT auto-enabled by the conversion. A classic-G/L customer has two valid paths: convert directly from classic G/L to S/4HANA, or first migrate classic G/L to New G/L and then convert. Customers still on Classic G/L must note that Foreign Currency Valuation, Line Item Display and Balance Carry Forward handling have changed in New G/L before migrating. READINESS ASSESSMENT: determine whether the customer is on Classic vs New G/L, and whether they intend to use Document Splitting / a ledger (parallel-ledger) approach — these drive a separate project beyond the technical conversion.
verified_findings.vote: merged from claims [4],[21],[22] — all unanimous 3-0; [4] primary-sourced, [21]/[22] blog-sourced but multiply corroborated

verified_findings.claim: Classic Credit Management (FI-AR-CR) is NOT available in S/4HANA; the mandatory functional equivalent is SAP Credit Management (FIN-FSCM-CR), BP-based with risk class on the business partner and release via Case Management. Migration is mandatory IF FI-AR-CR was used on the start release, and runs AFTER the technical SUM conversion (S4TWL note 2270544; conversion documented in the SAP Credit Management Configuration Guide). The IMG path is Migration to SAP S/4HANA Finance: Customizing under 'Preparations and Migration of Customizing > Preparatory Activities and Migration of Customizing for Credit Management' (first mandatory step 'Migrate Credit Management Customizing'); data under 'Data Migration > Credit Management Migration' (mandatory: Migrate Credit Management Master Data, Migrate Credit Management Exposure, Initialize Documented Credit Decisions, Reconcile Documented Credit Decisions). In the migration each credit control area becomes a credit segment with the SAME ID and each risk category becomes a risk class with the SAME ID. READINESS ASSESSMENT: detect FI-AR-CR usage — credit master maintained via FD31/FD32 in tables KNKK & KNKA, blocked-document transactions VKM1-VKM4 (VKM3 replaced by UKM_MY_DCDS), exposure in info structures S066/S067, and FM UKM_IS_ACTIVE returning space (FSCM not yet active). Master data moves to UKM_BP/BP; only credit check type D is supported.
verified_findings.vote: merged from claims [1],[5],[6],[7],[23],[24] — all unanimous 3-0; mix of primary config-guide and corroborated blog sources

verified_findings.claim: Bank Account Management (BAM) is the only compatible cash-management model in S/4HANA (S4TWL note 2870766 'Cash Management - BAM'); the classic Cash and Liquidity Management is not officially available. House bank accounts must be migrated BEFORE go-live, from classic table T012K into BAM master-data table FCLM_BAM_AMD, with FCLM_BAM_ACLINK2 linking bank accounts to house bank accounts (SAP-delivered migration structure FCLM_BAM_S_MIGRATION_T012K). Migration is done either MANUALLY via transaction FCLM_BAM_MIGRATION (per-account setting of account types) or AUTOMATICALLY via the central 'Start and Monitor Data Migration' activity CM1 (which sets all accounts to account type 01 / 'Activate Directly'; see SAP Note 2873947). Accounts are then maintained as new bank-account master data via the Manage Bank Accounts Fiori app on the Fiori Launchpad. The old house-bank maintenance transactions were unavailable prior to S/4HANA 1809; FI12 (House Bank/House Bank Account) was reintroduced from 1809. READINESS ASSESSMENT: detect populated T012/T012K house bank account configuration; any rows there require BAM migration before go-live.
verified_findings.vote: merged from claims [2],[17],[18] — all unanimous 3-0; primary S4TWL plus table-dictionary-verified blog facts

verified_findings.claim: The Finance migration cockpit (master conversion note 2332030, covering migration of GL, Asset Accounting, Controlling AND Material Ledger data to the new ACDOCA structure) executes AFTER the technical SUM conversion in a mandatory sequence: (1) FINS_MIG_PRECHECK ('Check Customizing Settings Prior to Migration') to clean inconsistencies; (2) 'Migrate General Customizing' (ledgers, currencies, CO integration) — must precede any manual IMG changes below it; (3) FINS_CUST_CONS_CHK ('Execute Consistency Check of General Ledger Settings') before migrating transactional data; (4) transactional data migration, monitored/resumed in transaction FINS_MIG_STATUS ('Start and Monitor Migration') and FINS_MIG_MONITOR_RC0, where step M10 migrates Material Ledger master data. Non-productive company codes can be excluded via the 'Template' flag in view V_001_TEMPLATE (SM30; objects T001-XTEMPLT/FINS_001_TEMPLT). Migration errors surfaced in FINS_MIG_STATUS must be resolved before go-live. This whole flow is gated by the SUM Simplification Item-Check (SI-Check), which runs at the start (RUN_S4H_SIF_CHECK_INIT — stops SUM on return code 12) and again just before downtime (RUN_S4H_SIF_CHECK_EXEC — stops on return code 8 or higher); Finance/GL/AA consistency items are enforced here. READINESS ASSESSMENT: run the Simplification Item-Check (SI-Check) pre-conversion and resolve all RC>=8 finance items before scheduling downtime.
verified_findings.vote: merged from claims [3],[8],[9],[10],[11],[12] — [3] split 2-1, the rest unanimous 3-0; predominantly primary-sourced

verified_findings.claim: MEHRWERK MPM (now mpmX) is built on the Qlik Sense platform, NOT natively on SAP HANA and NOT embedded in SAP Analytics Cloud — refuting the in-database/SAC-embedded hypothesis. It ingests SAP data via Qlik Sense connectors plus a proprietary MPM RuleEngine that extracts event logs OUT of SAP into Qlik's Associative Engine.

ARIS Process Mining (Software AG) connects to SAP ECC and S/4HANA (basis 700+) via a standalone on-premise 'Process Extractor' service using SAP JCo (>=3.1) over RFC. It requires importing a vendor-delivered transport (ProcessMiningTransport_v2.zip) that installs the /SOFWAG/MINING_V2 ABAP development class and function modules into SAP. The extractor polls ARIS Process Mining Cloud for tasks, extracts in chunks to local parquet files, and uploads over HTTPS — a clear extract-OUT (not in-SAP-stack) architecture.

IBM Process Mining (formerly myInvenio) extracts SAP data via an ABAP stage that auto-generates an ABAP extraction program, uploads it to the SAP server (optionally via the Change and Transport System / CTS), then invokes that program server-side at runtime to pull data back over RFC. This distinguishes it from connectors that only read tables via a generic RFC reader. IBM also ships a ready-to-use 'Accelerator for SAP Procure-to-Pay' performing ETL covering both Accounts Payable and Procurement.

QPR ProcessAnalyzer extracts SAP data via the SAP NetWeaver RFC Library 7.50, calling RFC function module BBP_RFC_READ_TABLE (with RFC_READ_TABLE as fallback) — a generic table-read mechanism requiring NO third-party component installed into SAP. It exposes two named methods: the ExtractSap function (expression language, where SAP table field names become output column names via a mandatory QueryTable parameter) and the --#ImportSapQuery command (SQL scripting).

Apromore (open-source-rooted) ingests SAP data via a no-code ETL 'Integration Center', shipping preconfigured extraction pipelines for order-to-cash (O2C), procure-to-pay (P2P), and record-to-report (R2R) with predefined table-to-log mappings, supporting both SAP ECC and S/4HANA.

Fluxicon Disco has NO built-in SAP connector. Its import page lists only generic file formats (CSV, MS Excel XLS/XLSX, MXML/MXML.GZ, XES/XES.GZ, FXL, DSC). SAP data must be exported to a flat file first (manually or via a third-party extractor like Transware Airlift) before Disco can ingest it.

Cross-cutting architecture map: NONE of the confirmed vendors run computation IN the SAP stack — all EXTRACT OUT. They split into (a) SAP-side-install RFC connectors that import a vendor transport / generate server-side ABAP (ARIS via /SOFWAG/MINING_V2 transport; IBM via auto-generated ABAP program), (b) zero-install generic table-read RFC connectors (QPR via BBP_RFC_READ_TABLE/RFC_READ_TABLE), (c) platform-mediated ETL/connector frameworks (MEHRWERK via Qlik connectors + RuleEngine; Apromore via no-code Integration Center ETL), and (d) no-native-connector file-import-only tools (Fluxicon Disco). The hypothesized in-database HANA / SAC-embedded model was found for NO vendor.

Context engineering = curating the optimal token set across the whole context state, a superset of prompt engineering. Context is FINITE and subject to 'context rot' (recall degrades as tokens grow: attention budget, n^2 relationships). Justifies tiered loading. [merges 0,1,16; 3-0]

ACTIONABLE: Just-in-time / progressive-disclosure. Agents hold lightweight identifiers (paths, queries, links) and load at runtime via tools, exploring layer by layer. Anthropic endorses HYBRID (small index up front + drill-down) = lean bootstrap index + graph_queries.py. [merges 2,6; 3-0]

ACTIONABLE: Three long-horizon techniques. COMPACTION (summarize+reinitialize) -> /compact + PreCompact hook. STRUCTURED NOTE-TAKING (notes outside context, pulled back) -> MEMORY.md/brain files. SUB-AGENTS (return condensed 1,000-2,000 token summary) -> Claude Code subagents. [claim 3; 3-0]

ACTIONABLE core primitive: Memory tool is CLIENT-SIDE, file-based under flat /memories the developer controls (file/db/cloud/encrypted backends), with exactly SIX ops: view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, rename. Full file ops, NOT key-value. Directly portable; model decides what/when to save. [merges 4,8,14; 3-0]

ACTIONABLE bootstrap hardening: Anthropic auto-injects (memory tool enabled) 'ALWAYS VIEW YOUR MEMORY DIRECTORY BEFORE DOING ANYTHING ELSE... ASSUME INTERRUPTION'. Confirms project's 'read brain_state.json first' as Anthropic's OWN guidance. Replicate in CLAUDE.md/SessionStart. [merges 5,14; 3-0]

SUPP, SCVE, SALA, BEXP, CHAR, RENT and GDDS are real ISO 20022 ExternalPurpose1Code values. SUPP=Supplier Payment · SCVE=Purchase & Sale of Services · SALA=Salary Payment · BEXP=Business Expenses · CHAR=Charity Payment · RENT=Rent · GDDS=Purchase & Sale of Goods. OTHR=Other exists as the explicit catch-all.

TRVL, RDEV, ITSV and TRAI are NOT ISO 20022 purpose codes. They do not appear in the official External Purpose Codes list (125 codes) nor in LHV's independent reference. There is no ISO code for research and development, for IT/telecom services as a purpose, or for training — the nearest real ones are SCVE for services, STDY for study, NWCH for network charge, and OTHR as catch-all.

The Central Bank of Egypt adopted ISO 20022 for interbank SWIFT messaging effective 2026-06-21, and the Egyptian RTGS has been upgraded to comply. This makes the ISO 20022 purpose-code family the correct one for Egypt rather than a national numeric list like Jordan's or India's.

No published Central Bank of Egypt purpose-of-payment CODE list was found. Searches across CBE, Citi and trade sources returned the ISO 20022 migration but no Egypt-specific code table. Consistent with the Citi notice, which asks for a DESCRIPTION and gives narrative examples rather than codes.

refuted_do_not_reassert.claim: Prior object-centric conformance approaches cannot adequately track object identity and object dependencies, so certain conformance violations in object-centric event logs go undetected — a gap this paper's identity-aware nets are designed to close.

The paper proposes a formalism-agnostic object-centric conformance checking approach via an abstraction layer called the 'object-centric state space', enabling comparable conformance results across multiple OC modelling formalisms (object-centric Petri nets, object-centric process trees, OC Petri nets with identifiers). This directly addresses the 'as-implemented vs as-delivered' conformance dimension where deviation = customization, but does so formalism-independent rather than by token replay/alignment on a single net.

The method detects new object-centric deviation types that prior techniques miss or hide, specifically 'missing objects' and 'mismatched object identities' in event execution, which existing OC conformance techniques either are insensitive to or fail to pinpoint to the deviating object. This is the deviation taxonomy a 'custom-over-standard' product needs to surface object-level customization.

HOEG (Heterogeneous Object Event Graph) encodes events and objects together into a single heterogeneous graph with diverse node types, without aggregating object features into event-level vectors, giving a more nuanced representation than prior object-centric encodings.

HOEG applies a heterogeneous Graph Neural Network architecture over object-centric event data to perform predictive process monitoring tasks (e.g., remaining-time prediction), directly demonstrating GNN-based predictive monitoring over object-centric logs.

OCPM² is a 12-stage object-centric process mining methodology grouped into five phases (Planning, Domain Modeling, Log Extraction, Analysis Iteration, Process Improvement & Support), extending PM²'s six stages for OCED extraction.

OCPM² defines an Extraction Matrix mapping object types to activities, and recommends documenting the relationship from a system perspective via CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations or, from a process perspective, via object quantity ranges per event.

Berti et al. extract object-centric event data from SAP ERP into OCEL by first constructing a Graph of Relations (GoR) over business-process tables, using a Python tool that identifies relevant tables and relationships; this informs OCPM²'s domain-modeling/extraction-matrix approach.

In OCPM², conformance checking, process discovery, and process enhancement live in the Mining & Analysis stage operating directly on the object-centric event log, producing compliance and performance findings; OCED can also be flattened to a traditional log to reuse classic techniques.

Object-Centric Process Mining can be enriched with four OLAP-inspired multi-dimensional operations (drill-down, roll-up, unfold, fold) that let analysts adjust the granularity of object-centric event logs, and applying drill-down/unfold measurably improves discovered process model fitness and precision.

The ocpa library can discover object-centric Petri nets (OCPN) from OCEL and compute their fitness and precision, but cannot do so for large logs or complex processes — i.e., object-centric conformance checking has a hard scalability ceiling on real industrial data.

The extraction approach classifies SAP tables into five classes, where 'change tables' (with CDHDR and CDPOS named as the primary change tables) are mined for events by transforming change records into activities via three methods: the change transaction code, the updated field name (e.g. 'Price Changed'), or a comparison of old vs new field values (e.g. 'Postpone Delivery').

The method builds a 'Graph of Relations' (GoR) — an undirected connected graph whose nodes are SAP tables and edges are shared join fields, centered on a master table most relevant to the target process, with node distance from the center encoding relevance — and relevant tables can be identified manually by domain experts, automatically by exploiting the SAP data dictionary table DD03VV to extract inter-table relationships, or by a hybrid of both.

The approach stores extracted SAP events as Object-Centric Event Logs (OCEL) precisely to avoid having to pick a single case notion, which resolves the convergence and divergence problems that afflict commercial SAP extractors (Celonis, ProcessGold) when a case notion such as order/item/delivery/invoice/payment must be fixed.

The RWTH PADS approach mines SAP business events primarily from the change-document tables CDHDR and CDPOS, defining each event by explicit filter criteria over CDPOS fields — e.g. an event is generated only when CDPOS.OBJECTCLAS='EINKBELEG' and CDPOS.CHNGIND='I', or for a field change when CDPOS.FNAME='FRGZU', CDPOS.VALUE_OLD='X', CDPOS.VALUE_NEW='XX' — with the timestamp built from CDHDR.UDATE + CDHDR.UTIME. This is a directly reusable recipe for turning SAP change documents into OCEL events.

The method introduces an 'Extraction Blueprint' that maps joined SAP tables to object-centric 'activity concepts' (which table entries become which events, with related objects, timestamp, activity name, and filter criteria), and was implemented on a real SAP system pulling from tables JCDS, TJ02T, AFKO, RESB, CDPOS, CDHDR, EBAN, EKBE, MSEG (plus EKKO/EKPO/AUFK), using the open-source sap-extractor project into pandas dataframes.

Object-centric conformance against a normative/base process model surfaces customization and policy deviations: comparing the as-implemented event log to the base model via object-centric fitness yielded 0.9275 (vs a perfect 1.0), and discovering an OCPN exposed a silent transition allowing the mandatory second purchase-requisition release to be skipped — diagnosed as a conformance problem because the second release should be mandatory per company rule.

The method discovers the relevant SAP source tables via a Graph of Relations (GoR) — an undirected connected graph whose nodes are SAP tables holding the candidate process information — which is the mechanism that can be seeded from a custom master table to traverse to related (including Z) tables.

The approach produces Object-Centric Event Logs (OCEL) where a single event can be linked to multiple typed objects, avoiding a forced single case notion — directly relevant to object-centric SAP process mining.

SAP Signavio Process Insights ships ready-to-use reference process flows with preconfigured performance metrics and benchmarks, providing a normative baseline for monitoring SAP processes out of the box.

The product contains a built-in library of over 1,000 typical issues/inefficiencies that it detects and prioritizes automatically across SAP process domains (financial, manufacturing, quality, maintenance, service, claims, capex).

The method derives events primarily from SAP change tables CDHDR and CDPOS (the change-document mechanism), classifying SAP tables into roles: transaction tables (TCODE executions), change tables (CDHDR/CDPOS), record/master tables (e.g. EKKO), and detail tables — i.e. its extraction layer is change-document-based, not redo-log or RFC-streaming based.
PM4Py ships no native SAP connector or SAP table-to-event-log extractor; SAP integration must be built by practitioners on top of the library (e.g., custom BKPF/BSEG/CDHDR-to-XES recipes).

CVI_MIGRATION_PRECHK is a CVI migration consistency-check report whose results are viewed via transaction CVI_PRECHK; the two are paired as the check runner and its result viewer for Business Partner / Customer-Vendor Integration readiness.

SAP Readiness Check analyzes six areas: add-on/extension compatibility, custom ABAP code impact (including deprecated functions), sizing and performance, business process transformation, recommended Fiori apps, and an aggregated SAP Note Analyzer input file.

The Simplification Item Check (referenced as the S4TC 'Conversion & Upgrade new Simplification Item Checks') identifies version-specific simplification items, flags mandatory changes that must be addressed, and verifies technical prerequisites (kernel updates, database requirements) before conversion.

SAP GRC Access Control stores its SoD ruleset across five core tables: GRACFUNC (business functions), GRACFUNCACT (function-to-action links), GRACFUNCPRM (action-to-permission maps), GRACSODRULE (conflicting function/action/permission combinations), and GRACSODRISK (identified user violations).

GRACSODRISK is the violation output table populated during a risk-analysis run, listing users who currently hold conflicting access, distinguishing the rule-definition tables from the analysis-result table.
IBM's SAP data extraction is built on SAP's Remote Function Call (RFC) protocol — the proprietary SAP protocol used to exchange data with SAP systems — rather than CDS views or OData.

QPR ProcessAnalyzer's ExtractSap function connects to SAP via the RFC (Remote Function Call) interface, calling SAP function modules RFC_READ_TABLE (default) or BBP_RFC_TABLE to extract table data directly.

Disco's only data-ingestion path is a manual mapping import ('Smart log import') that maps generic CSV/Excel columns to Case ID, Activity, Timestamp, Resource, and other attributes — i.e., SAP data must be exported to a flat file first by an external extractor before Disco can use it.
QPR ProcessAnalyzer's SAP connector is compatible with all SAP R/3 (ECC), SAP S/4HANA, and SAP HANA versions, giving it broad coverage across legacy and modern SAP landscapes.

The public QPR connectors page does NOT document the specific technical extraction mechanism (ScriptLauncher, SQL-based ETL, RFC, BAPI, or named table reads), so the ScriptLauncher + SQL-ETL architecture asserted for QPR is not confirmed by this primary source and remains publicly undocumented on this page.

mindzie studio's documented dataset-loading method is manual file upload supporting CSV, XES, and Binary formats — not an automated SAP connector. The load-dataset workflow consists of uploading a file, then mapping columns to Case ID, Activity, and Activity Time via drag-and-drop.

mindzie does advertise out-of-the-box system connectors that include SAP (alongside Microsoft Dynamics, Oracle, NetSuite, JD Edwards, Salesforce, HubSpot), but the marketing material names SAP only as a logo/system in the connector list without describing the SAP-specific extraction mechanism.

Theobald Xtract Universal extracts SAP table data via a custom function module /THEO/READ_TABLE, which is installed into SAP to improve performance and bypass restrictions of SAP's standard RFC_READ_TABLE function module.

UiPath Process Mining ingests SAP data using Theobald Xtract Universal (XU), a third-party SAP-certified extraction tool that connects to SAP source systems via Remote Function Calls (RFC) — i.e., UiPath does NOT use its own native SAP connector for this path but relies on Theobald.

The Theobald Xtract Universal extraction mechanism installs a read-only custom ABAP function module named Z_THEO_READ_TABLE into the SAP system, which is the named connector/table-read mechanism used to pull SAP table data.

In Anthropic's Managed Agents platform, a memory store is a workspace-scoped collection of small text documents that persists across sessions — i.e., cross-session continuity is implemented as durable text files, not opaque vectors.

Managed Agents memory is mounted as a real filesystem directory (at /mnt/memory/<store-name>/) and the agent reads/writes it with standard file tools (bash, read, write, edit, glob, grep) — confirming the pattern is portable to a file-based Claude Code setup that uses the same primitives.

Auto memory uses a tiered/hierarchical load model: only the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md (whichever comes first) is loaded into every session; topic files are NOT loaded at startup and are read on demand. This is the canonical Claude Code tiered-loading pattern to emulate for a brain.

CLAUDE.md files (unlike MEMORY.md) are loaded in FULL at launch regardless of length, and @path imports do NOT reduce context because imported files also load at launch — so a large CLAUDE.md/brain bootstrap directly consumes context every session. The portable fix is path-scoped rules, which load only when matching files are read.

Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ with YAML `paths` frontmatter load into context only when Claude reads files matching the glob pattern; rules without `paths` load unconditionally at launch with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md. This is a native progressive-disclosure mechanism for a file-based CLI setup.

Egypt requires a national purpose-of-payment code list comparable to Jordan's CBJ codes or India's RBI codes. No such published list was found, and the bank's own notice asks for a free-text description instead.
